elements.text: A Dual-Constraint Agentic Workflow for Pet-Friendly Balcony and Courtyard Planting Design

CHEN Niannian  |  26063619G
COMP5511: Artificial Intelligence Concepts
The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
"Beautiful for you. Fatal for your cat."
700+ ornamental species are dangerous to cats or dogs -- and LLMs recommend them, because toxicity is a fact the model cannot check for itself.
Need a defensible first draft, fast.
Need one design that satisfies every constraint at once.

Horticultural viability
   light + moisture must suit the site

Veterinary safety
   no species toxic to the household pets

Design space
   balcony / courtyard / rooftop terrace
Both constraints must hold simultaneously, for every species in the scheme.
Method: split the task by what can be checked
If a constraint can be checked deterministically, the LLM should not be allowed to decide it.
LLM reads the brief -> pets, light class, moisture class
Python removes every species toxic to a household pet
LLM composes zones, combination logic, care and cautions
Python re-checks safety and a 15-item design rubric
Violations and missing rubric items go back to the model
Ground truth and the decision rules

A species toxic to any pet in the household is removed before the model ever sees the candidate list.

Toxicity labels come from the ASPCA Animal Poison Control database, one source URL per species.

Light is stored as the darkest light a plant tolerates: full shade < bright indirect < partial shade < full sun. A plant is viable when the site is at least as bright as its tolerance.

If the strict query is empty, moisture is relaxed first, then light -- and the relaxation is reported to the user.
How the three methods are compared
One prompt. The model answers from memory, with no catalogue and no filter.
Top-k retrieved species are passed to the model. Nothing is excluded.
Retrieval + negative filtering + deterministic audit with repair loops.
Identical output contract for all three
Same JSON schema, same required design content, same rubric. Only grounding and filtering differ -- so the comparison measures the architecture, not the prompt.

1 Pet safety
2 Horticultural viability
3 Dual-constraint accuracy
4 Design completeness (0-15)
5 Out-of-database rate

Fill from results/summary.csv
Safety = pet-safety compliance, Viab. = horticultural viability, Compl. = design completeness 0-15, O-o-DB = out-of-database rate.
The agent's pet-safety compliance is exactly 100%, because the filter is deterministic -- the model is never given the opportunity to pick an unsafe species.
Design quality is a separate axis from safety
The rubric is code, not opinion

15 binary items, each with a stored detection rule:

A1-A3  three spatial zones (vertical, ground, pet-accessible)
C2-C3  watering frequency + light position  ->  core score 0-5

A vague mention scores nothing.
A design must also explain itself
spatial structure  /  combination logic  /  care instructions  /  care cautions -- each with a per-item failure list fed back to the model for one repair round.
Limitations I want to state myself

150 of 1000+ listed species
Cats and dogs only
25 scenarios -- a defensible scale, not a large one
A mis-parsed brief propagates into the candidate pool
The guarantee covers species in the database; the out-of-database rate is reported separately

Dense recall + deterministic filtering
Per-species provenance shown in the answer
Iterative tool use with iterative auditing
More species, more pets, more site types

The takeaway: swap in a stronger LLM and the design gets prettier; the toxicity guarantee does not move.
Every checkable constraint belongs in code.
The LLM designs; deterministic code decides what is allowed, and checks what came back.
